## Files users attach to a chat

Users can attach a file to a message with the paperclip in the chat input, by dragging it onto the input, or by pasting it. Accepted formats are `csv`, `tsv`, `txt`, `md`, `json`, `jsonl`, `yaml`, `xml`, `html`, `sql`, `pdf`, `xls`, `xlsx`, `docx` and `parquet`, plus PNG, JPEG, GIF and WebP images.

An attachment is uploaded before the message is sent and lands in the sender's own space, under a folder named after the day:

```text
/home/uploads/2026-08-04/sales.csv
```

The agent then treats it like any other saved file: it is listed by `list`, found by `search`, and read by `read`. A second upload of the same name on the same day is suffixed (`sales-2.csv`) rather than replacing the earlier one.

**The agent is only told the path, never the contents.** This is the important part: a 9 MB CSV costs nothing in context until the agent decides to read it, and a large attachment can never push the conversation out of the context window on arrival. The agent reads, greps or queries the file when the question actually needs what is inside.

<Info>
Images are the exception, and are handled the other way round. An image is attached to be *interpreted*, so it is stored with the conversation and sent to the model inline - it is not written to permanent storage, and does not appear in `/home`.
</Info>

Spreadsheets, PDFs, Word documents and Parquet files cannot be read as text. `read` refuses them with an explanation rather than pouring binary into the conversation; the agent parses them with `execute_python` when [Python execution](/nao-agent/chat/capabilities/tools-mcps-skills) is enabled, and otherwise asks for a CSV export.

<Note>
Attaching files needs permanent storage. With `NAO_STORAGE_BACKEND=none` the paperclip only accepts images, and the size limit is the one set by `NAO_STORAGE_MAX_FILE_SIZE_MB`. A message carries at most 5 attachments, and an image at most 5 MB.
</Note>

<Warning>
Viewers cannot upload files, for the same reason they cannot send messages.

The chat UI can render agent query results as charts (bar, line, area, pie, donut, KPI card, scatter, radar, and stacked variants) or as tables with conditional formatting. Both can be edited after the fact, and every chart exposes the SQL query and rows behind it.

You can attach images directly in the chat input when you want the agent to inspect a screenshot, dashboard, chart, or UI state. There are three ways to add images to a message:

- Click the `+` menu in the chat input and pick **Upload image**.
- Drag an image file from your desktop into the chat input - the input shows a highlighted drop zone while you drag.

- Up to **5 MB** per image.

Images you've sent stay attached to the message and re-display when the chat is reloaded or shared. Click any image in the conversation to open it in a full-size lightbox - close it with `Esc`, the X button, or by clicking outside.

export const pdfSkill: InternalSkill = {
	name: 'pdf-handling',
	description:
		'How to get data out of a PDF, and what to do when the usual read does not work: scanned files with no text layer, tables whose layout is lost, and figures that need reading as an image. Load this before working with a .pdf file.',
	body: `# Working with PDFs

Reading a PDF with **read** gives you its text layer, page by page, prefixed with a
\`--- Page N ---\` marker and a header saying how many pages the file has. Start there. The rest
of this skill is about the cases where that is not enough.

## Trust the page count

The header tells you the true number of pages; the body may be cut short because a long read is
truncated. If the last marker you can see is well below the page count, you have not read the
whole document. Say so rather than answering as if you had, and read again with a narrower goal
or work through a sandbox.

## A PDF with no text layer

A scanned document — a photographed invoice, a signed contract, an old report — has no text
layer, and **read** fails saying so. It is not a corrupt file and re-reading will not help.

Two ways forward, in order of preference:

1. If the user also attached the page as an **image**, read the image instead: you can see images
   directly, and that is the fastest route for one or two pages.
2. Otherwise tell the user plainly that the PDF is scanned and its text cannot be extracted, and
   ask whether they can supply the underlying data (a CSV, an export, the original spreadsheet).
   Offer OCR only if a sandbox is available, and warn that OCR on a table is unreliable.

Never guess at the contents of a scanned PDF from its filename.

## Tables and layout

PDF has no concept of a table: what looks like a grid is absolutely-positioned text, and
extraction flattens it into lines. Numbers may end up separated from their labels, columns may
interleave, and a figure like \`1,234\` may arrive split.

So: read a PDF to *understand* a document, quote from it, or find where something is stated. Do
not treat extracted rows as data to compute with. If a user wants totals, growth, or any figure
you would have to recompute, either

- take the numbers the document itself states, and say which page they came from, or
- ask for the data behind the report,
- or parse it properly in a sandbox (below).

Never silently transcribe a PDF table into a chart or a SQL insert. A transcription error in a
financial table is the kind of mistake that destroys trust in every other number you produce.

## Parsing properly in a sandbox

When \`execute_sandboxed_code\` is available and the document really has to be parsed, mount the
file with \`storage_files\` and use a library built for the job:

\`\`\`
storage_files: ["/home/uploads/2026-01-31/report.pdf"]
packages: ["pdfplumber"]
\`\`\`

\`\`\`python
import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("files/uploads/2026-01-31/report.pdf") as pdf:
    page = pdf.pages[3]
    for table in page.extract_tables():
        for row in table:
            print(row)
\`\`\`

\`pdfplumber\` keeps column structure far better than a plain text extract, which is the whole
reason to bother with a sandbox. Print what you found and check it looks like a table before you
use it. For a scanned file you would need OCR instead (\`pytesseract\` plus the \`tesseract-ocr\`
system package), which is slow and often wrong on numbers — get the user's agreement first.

---
title: Local Database
description: Query files and earlier results with nao's built-in DuckDB, and join the two
---

Alongside your warehouses, nao ships a **DuckDB instance of its own**. The agent reaches it by passing a reserved database id to `execute_sql`:

```sql
-- database_id: duckdb_local
SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM read_csv('/home/uploads/2026-08-04/sales.csv')
GROUP BY region
ORDER BY revenue DESC
```

It is always available, needs no configuration, and exists because two useful questions have no warehouse to ask:

- **What is in this file?** A CSV, JSON, Parquet or Excel file is queried where it sits, whether the user attached it to a message or the agent saved it earlier.
- **What if I reshape what I already have?** Every result in the chat is a table named after its query id, so a follow-up can pivot or aggregate rows without going back to the warehouse.

And the reason both matter at once: **a file can be joined to warehouse data.**

## Joining a file to your warehouse

This is what the local database is really for. A user attaches a spreadsheet of targets and asks how the quarter went against it. The agent queries the warehouse for actuals, then joins the file to that result:

```sql
-- database_id: duckdb_local
SELECT t.region, t.target, a.actual, a.actual - t.target AS variance
FROM read_xlsx('/home/uploads/2026-08-04/targets.xlsx') t
JOIN query_ab12cd34 a USING (region)
ORDER BY variance
```

`query_ab12cd34` is the id returned by the earlier `execute_sql` call against the warehouse. Results from previous turns work too, and the query result is a normal one: it gets its own id, and charts and tables can be built from it.

<Info>
The file never enters the conversation. The agent sends a path, DuckDB reads the bytes, and only the rows the query returns come back - so a 9 MB CSV can be aggregated without spending any context on its contents.
</Info>

## Reading files

Paths work exactly as they do everywhere else in the agent's file tree: `/home/...` for [saved files](/nao-agent/self-hosting/permanent-storage), and project context paths for files in the context folder.

| Format | Function |
|---|---|
| CSV, TSV | `read_csv('/home/uploads/sales.csv')` |
| JSON, JSONL | `read_json('/home/exports/events.jsonl')` |
| Parquet | `read_parquet('/home/data/orders.parquet')` |
| Excel | `read_xlsx('/home/uploads/budget.xlsx', sheet = 'FY26')` |

On the `local` storage backend, wildcards work too (`read_csv('/home/exports/*.csv')`). On `s3` each file is named explicitly, because the files are fetched from the bucket before the query runs.

<Note>
Excel support comes from DuckDB's `excel` extension, which the official Docker image bakes in at build time. `read_xlsx` reads the first sheet and assumes the first row is the header, so the agent is told to check the shape of a sheet before trusting it - and to fall back to the sandbox and pandas for a messy workbook.
</Note>

## What it cannot do

The query is written by a model, so DuckDB is locked down before it runs. In order: file access is narrowed to the directories the query legitimately needs, everything else external is switched off, and the configuration is locked so the query cannot undo either step.

The practical effect:

- **Only the user's own files.** The allowlist is built per query from that user's storage space plus the project folder. Another user's files are unreachable even by their real path on disk, and so is the rest of the filesystem.
- **No network.** No HTTP reads, no S3 URLs, no extension downloads.
- **Read-only.** `COPY ... TO`, `ATTACH` and any write statement are rejected. To produce a file, the agent uses `write` or the sandbox.
- **No widening.** `SET allowed_directories`, `SET enable_external_access` and friends fail once the query is running.

<Info>
`/home` is a virtual path. Each user's `/home` resolves to a different real location, and that translation happens per query - which is also what the file allowlist is built from.
</Info>

## When the warehouse is still the right answer

The local database is for files and for results already in hand. A question the warehouse can answer on its own should go to the warehouse: it has the indexes, the full history, and none of the transfer. The agent is told this, and reaches for `duckdb_local` when a file is involved or when it is reshaping something it already fetched.

Done. `execute_sql` now takes a reserved `database_id: "duckdb_local"` that runs the query in nao's own DuckDB, with the per-user `allowed_directories` approach you asked for.

**How the translation works.** Before DuckDB sees anything, the query's string literals are walked and every `/home/...` (or `~/...`) path is rewritten to where that file really lives, which differs per user and per backend. Those same paths determine the jail. On the `local` backend the user's storage root is handed over as-is, so wildcards keep working; on `s3` there is no filesystem, so only the named files are staged into a temp directory that dies with the request. Then, in the order your probe proved is the only one that works: `LOAD excel` → `SET allowed_directories` → `SET enable_external_access = false` → `SET lock_configuration = true`. Query-result tables are created before the lockdown so the temp workspace never needs to be inside the jail.

The test suite in `apps/backend/tests/local-query.test.ts` asserts the posture end to end, including the case that matters most for a multi-user instance: user A naming user B's real path on disk is refused, and the same `/home/notes.csv` resolves to a different file for each of them.

Three things worth flagging beyond the plan:

- **Numbers were coming back as strings.** DuckDB renders BIGINT and DECIMAL as text so JSON keeps their precision, which meant a `COUNT(*)` would reach a chart as `"3"`. Values are now converted back to numbers unless they genuinely cannot survive a JavaScript number, in which case they stay text. This also fixes the pre-existing `runSqlOverQueryResults` path, so three of its assertions changed from `'3'` to `3`.
- **The excel skill was telling the agent something now false** — that the sandbox was "exactly one way in" and that it could not produce an `.xlsx`. It now picks between the local database for a tidy sheet and pandas for a messy one, with the tell I found while verifying the extension: columns named `A1`, `B1`… mean DuckDB found no header row.
- **Sandbox files can now be kept.** `save_files` copies from `out/` in the VM into `/home`, which is what makes a generated workbook outlive the sandbox.

I verified the Docker side rather than assuming it: with the extension baked into a directory and `HOME` pointed at an empty dir, `read_xlsx` works offline inside the jail while reading outside it, writing out, and `INSTALL`ing anything further are all blocked.
